extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in Hugo Awards, science fiction/fantasy awards, and fandom controversies
extracted.subtask_short: hugo awards nomination and voting rules
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and eligibility rules for the Hugo Awards: who can nominate and vote, what makes a work eligible, how ballots are formed, the instant-runoff voting system, use of 'No Award', and timeline for nominations and final voting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hugo Award eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Works are eligible for an award if they were published in the prior calendar year, or translated into English in the prior calendar year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies across Hugo categories (written and dramatic works). Eligibility is tied to publication/translation timing (prior calendar year).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who nominates and votes (membership requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hugo Award nominees and winners are chosen by supporting or attending members of the annual World Science Fiction Convention (Worldcon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only supporting or attending Worldcon members participate in nominations and final voting; membership status therefore determines who can influence ballot composition and winners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination limits and ballot formation
rubrics_metrics.description: During the period the Sad Puppies campaign was active, the ballot consisted of five works for each category that were the most-nominated by members that year, with each member being able to nominate five works per category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial nominations are made by members (each may nominate up to five works per category); the five most-nominated works become the final ballot in that category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination and final voting timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial nominations were made by members in January through March, while voting on the ballot of five nominations was performed roughly in April through July, subject to change depending on when that year's Worldcon is held.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worldcons are generally held near the start of September; timelines can shift with Worldcon scheduling. Organizers and participants should plan around these windows for eligibility and campaigning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection process — instant-runoff voting with five nominees
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection process is defined in the WSFS constitution as instant-runoff voting with five nominees per category, except in the case of a tie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final ballots present up to five nominees and are resolved by instant-runoff rules (ranked-choice elimination). Ties may alter the number of nominees in exceptional cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and guidance for 'No Award' ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: For each category of Hugo, the voter may rank 'No Award' as one of their choices. Voters are instructed that they should do so if they feel that none of the nominees are worthy of the award, or if they feel the category should be abolished entirely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A vote for 'No Award' other than as one's first choice signifies that the voter believes the nominees ranked higher than 'No Award' are worthy of a Hugo in that category, while those ranked lower are not. 'No Award' can therefore be used to remove categories or indicate all nominees are unworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballot composition: most-nominated works determine finalists
rubrics_metrics.description: The final ballot for each category consists of the works that received the most nominations from members during the nomination period (five nominees per category under the system described).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because finalists are determined by raw nomination counts, coordinated nomination slates (voting blocs) can disproportionately influence which works appear on the final ballot unless rules or safeguards counteract that effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule changes to limit slate/bloc voting
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominating rules for the Hugos were changed (effective for the 2017 awards) to limit the power of bloc voting for small sets of works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rule changes were introduced in response to slate campaigns (Sad Puppies/Rabid Puppies) and are intended to reduce the ability of organized slates to dominate final ballot composition; the article notes the change but does not detail the specific amendments.
